idiom_name: per-type builder: safe defaults + named overrides + real-constructor build
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: for each domain type, initialise one field per constructor parameter with a commonly used, safe value, expose an override step that is named after the field (withX(...), or the language's copy-with/update idiom) and a terminal build that constructs the product through its real constructor so no invariant is bypassed. Add one static factory per type - aUser(), anInvoice() - as the syntactic sugar that makes tests read like the domain, and a but()/copy helper so tests can derive a similar object from an existing builder or instance. Nest builders for related types instead of flattening the graph, treat each builder as single-use, and keep the whole construction in test sources.
code_sketch:
builder = a_user()                       # valid defaults
builder.with_email("bad@example.com")    # state only what the test asserts
user = builder.build()                   # real constructor, validation intact
# or, where the language supports copy-with:
# user = a_user().copy(email="bad@example.com")
pitfalls: Skipping the build step and letting tests reach into the builder's fields re-couples the test to the object's structure.
Defaults duplicated per test instead of per type recreate the duplication the pattern removes.
A builder whose defaults never go through the product's validation produces objects the domain cannot represent.

Wrong move: asserting on a value that came from a default no test mentions -> editing that default silently changes what every such test expects -> instead assert only on values the test set explicitly, or have the test override the field it depends on.

Wrong move: reusing one builder instance across tests and mutating it per test -> earlier overrides leak into later cases and failures become order-dependent -> instead take a fresh builder from the static factory in every test and derive similar objects via a but()/copy helper.

Wrong move: importing the test builder into production because its default factory was convenient -> the test-chosen defaults become the product's implicit specification and production now depends on test sources -> instead keep the builder in the test sources and let production keep its own constructors.
